newsitem.title: FRANCE: Baby slain in Algerian village massacre - papers.
newsitem.headline: Baby slain in Algerian village massacre - papers.

text.p: A six-month-old baby was among 18 people massacred by Moslem rebels in the third raid on an Algerian village where people said the authorities refused them weapons to defend themsleves, Algerian newspapers said on Tuesday.

Liberte newspaper quoted a survivor of the Sunday night attack on Douaouda village, 60 km (40 miles) west of the capital Algiers as saying the villagers had asked the government for arms to defend themselves from guerrillas after earlier raids.
"We are unfortunate poor people and this is the reason why we are let down. They (the authorities) did not want to give us arms," the villager said.
Liberte said among the victims was a six-month-old baby whose throat had been slit when scores of Moslem guerrillas came down into Douaouda from the surrounding Chrea mountains.
When the killings were reported by the security forces on Monday, they said the people had been "assassinated in a cowardly way" -- the term used when rebels slit throats.
Le Matin quoted eyewitnesses as saying 27 people were slaughtered in the Douaouda raid, the third in two months on the village.
The newspaper named one of the rebels as Hakim Dendani, from the village, who it said was an aide to Algeria's ruthless Armed Islamic Group (GIA) guerrilla chief Antar Zouabri.
One villager told Liberte that farmers in the village were unable to tend their farms because of the violence in the area.
"Six hundred hectares (1,500 acres) of land suitable for cultivation has been abandoned since the armed groups began holding sway in the region," he said.
Le Matin said the rebel attack had "demolished Prime Minister (Ahmed Ouyahia's) optimism" about crushing the guerrillas.

Ouyahia said in a weekend speech that "terrorism has really been reduced to a residual level". His comment came just at the start of a 24-hour period of violence in Algeria, when at least 38 people were killed by rebels, including the 18 in Douaouda.

Moslem hardliners plunged Algeria in violence early in 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election that radical Islamists were poised to win. About 60,000 people, including more than 100 foreigners, have been killed in the conflict.
